title: Universities must be partners in the devolution agenda
summary: Luke Green and Liz Shutt make the case that to make devolution a success, civic universities need to partner more and lead less
full_text:
As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was extolling the virtues of devolution, and the role universities can play in powering up local economies, long before he became Prime Minister.

For a sector navigating turbulent times, the devolution agenda offers a rare glimmer of hope. Universities’ relationship with Whitehall has often proven choppy, buffeted by changes in government direction and shifting political currents. Their ties with local and regional governments have tended to make for smoother sailing: mayors, councils and regional policymakers usually have a more rounded understanding of what universities bring to a place, and a greater stake in seeing those contributions endure.

If more power is heading out of Whitehall and into towns, cities and regions, as the government’s plans to “rewire the state” suggest, the assumption is that universities will surely benefit.

Certainly, the promised transfer of policy functions to regional authorities will provide further ground for universities to collaborate with their places on defining their local policy challenges and helping to address them. And as Peter O’Brien, Jane Robinson, and Helen Turner have recently highlighted, there is a huge amount of existing work and expertise on how to do this.

Yet, amid the devo-mania, there is a danger that universities draw the wrong lesson regarding the role they should play.

Anchors away

For the best part of fifteen years, the civic university agenda has increasingly become a university leadership agenda. Universities have been encouraged to see themselves as anchor institutions, convenors, and civic leaders. They have been cast as the organisations capable of stepping into the gaps left by years of local government austerity and institutional decline.

In many places, universities have genuinely been among the few organisations with the capacity and resources to take on those roles. They have embraced the opportunity to prove their value as civic institutions, and begun to shed their reputation as ivory towers detached from the communities around them.

But the challenges facing places rarely fit neatly within institutional boundaries. They increasingly require forms of civic leadership that can align democratic institutions, public services, businesses, anchor organisations and communities around shared priorities. As powers and responsibilities are devolved across places, effective civic leadership will depend on the capacity to connect these different institutions and interests.

Universities have an important part to play in this wider civic endeavour. But that does not necessarily mean taking the lead. As we argue in a new open access article with Sarah Chaytor, Louise Kempton, and John Tomaney, universities may be most effective when they support and strengthen wider civic capacity: contributing expertise, evidence, convening power and long-term commitment to place.

All hands on deck

A local leadership mindset encourages universities to start with themselves: What expertise do we have? What assets can we deploy? What initiative can we launch? Yet places rarely experience their challenges in those terms.

A civic mindset starts somewhere else: what does this place need, and who is best placed to provide it? Sometimes that will be a university. Sometimes it will not.

That is what a genuine partnership approach requires. Universities become one civic actor among many, rather than assuming they should sit at the centre of every conversation. The emphasis shifts from institutional visibility to shared outcomes, and from launching initiatives to building relationships and capacity that can endure.

This matters because the civic university’s biggest problem has never really been a shortage of activity. It has been a shortage of co-ordination and embeddedness.

Scratch beneath the surface and much civic work depends on a handful of committed individuals, a sympathetic senior leader, or a funding stream that might not exist in three years’ time. Launching a new initiative is relatively straightforward. Building trust across a place over ten or twenty years is not. Signing a civic agreement is only the start. Changing governance arrangements, incentives and institutional priorities so that civic engagement survives beyond a particular vice chancellor or funding programme is considerably harder.

Partnership, in other words, is harder than leadership – and its rewards are often much less visible.

And that brings us to Manchesterism.

The real lesson of Manchesterism

The Greater Manchester story is often told as a story about leadership. Burnham’s meteoric rise helps reinforce that narrative. But the deeper lesson of Greater Manchester is about what can happen when institutions develop the capacity to work collaboratively over time.

Whatever criticisms one might make of Manchesterism, its successes have been built on decades of collaboration between local authorities, public services, businesses and universities. Its strength comes less from any one institution leading than from a range of institutions finding ways to work together around shared priorities.

Universities have been an important part of that story. But they have generally been most effective when helping to strengthen the wider civic ecosystem rather than positioning themselves at its centre.

As devolution expands across England, that is the lesson other places ought to learn.

The most valuable contribution universities can make is not to become more prominent local leaders. It is to become better civic partners: more embedded in their places, more willing to share power and more focused on the slow, often unglamorous, under-recognised work of building relationships and collective capacity.

If devolution succeeds, it will not be because universities took a leading role. It will be because they helped make collective leadership possible.

title: Can a dashboard solve higher education planning?
summary: OfS has built one dashboard to rule them all - DK has thoughts
full_text:
Have you ever wondered what higher education provision is on offer in your area? Have you ever wondered whether there was a measure of demand for these courses?

And do you ever wonder what research is going on near you?

To be clear, if it is your job to manage such within your provider, you probably do. If you work on developing a vocational course portfolio, or relationships with employers, or research collaborations, this is information that you can see by looking at your institutional dashboards, or what is pinned to your office wall.

But the Skills White Paper promised a full-on market monitoring function – something aimed as much at the world around Skills England and local skills partnerships as the higher education sector. And this morning the Office for Students published a “prototype” of this dashboard, for sector feedback.

What OfS has released?

There’s already open data available on student recruitment by provider (UCAS), students on higher education courses by provider (HESA), student loans by provider (SLC) and student outcomes (OfS B3, Graduate Outcomes, LEO). OfS’ new dashboard also adds in information about research capabilities, which it derives from commercial data on research funding and research outputs published by Elsevier.

I’m guessing that the inclusion of the latter (along with some TRAC-related information that is merged into the research data) is why OfS has departed from Official Statistics best practice by choosing not to publish the underlying data alongside the dashboard. We are promised that this will arrive alongside future iterations of the tool – which will be determined by feedback from users.

So what we do get is what amounts to a series of tabs (one per data source) summarising information either by provider, or in some case by local area (ILTS1 region, ILTS2 region, LSIP region). The default is to allow the user to view changes in key variables over time – there are some maps linked to student uptake which largely duplicate what HESA has already published.

What’s missing?

While any release of data is welcome, it feels like OfS is not getting the maximum value from these sources. This is because of a curious design choice.

For me, the value of data from multiple sources is the ability to cross-tabulate them in order to answer questions of strategic value. For instance, do areas that are research active in a particular subject also offer good teaching in that subject? Which universities recruit locally and which are more focused on bringing students into a local area? Where are (as the British Academy has investigated) subject cold spots, and which providers have the potential to fill them?

The OfS dashboard keeps each source of data separate – it is best understood as a set of complementary dashboards rather than a single entity. It is a way of allowing people to explore each of these datasets, but it doesn’t allow for the kind of analysis that combining them should be able to bring.

In part, this is understandable – different data sources use different standards (especially geographically and in defining subject areas) which makes it complicated to compare like with like. League table compilers famously struggle to include research data (which generally maps to either cost centres or REF units of assessment) while also using teaching data (which these days pretty much standardised to CAH): there is not a reliable mapping between these standards.

But it is not impossible – especially when you are an arms-length body with the ability to see and use all kinds of data not routinely available to mortals like ourselves, and even specify how it is organised. My suspicion is that the choice and nature of this release is defensive, in that it does not require data other than what is routinely published (or purchasable) – making this choice unfortunately limits the ability to provide new insight. OfS should use this exercise as an opportunity to consider what data is currently published and how it is made available.

We also do not get the promised information on research infrastructure – the research section of the dashboard is sub-optimal for reasons that I will get to – but it is a shame not to look at what kit is available where given that Jisc runs the marvellous Equipment Data Service that holds this data.

Why is OfS trying to do this now?

The impetus for this market monitoring dashboard comes from the Skills White Paper. The plan was to “provide a clear, single picture of higher education supply and demand” in order to “highlight any gaps between demand, supply and local need.” It is very much of a piece with the work of Skills England (there’s a local skills dashboard, for example) that aims to inform the work of local skills improvement partnerships (LSIPs) in understanding what provision needs to be commissioned to meet local industry needs.

Situating skills and training decisions in local areas is one of the key themes in the government’s devolution agenda – and Labour’s decision to actively include higher education (as a skills provider as well as an employment sector) means that the sector is much more engaged in this work. The aim of the dashboard, therefore, is to offer an approachable single source of truth to inform these local discussions.

Data like this also has the potential to be used in national planning (although opinions are variable as to whether we have any chance of doing that). There’s been rumblings about a retooling of the OfS strategic priorities grant (SBG) to focus on national priorities rather than “high cost” subjects, and you’d imagine that data like this would add a local or regional aspect to decision making. It is possible that OfS could directly address cold spots on a subject-by-subject basis via the use of financial incentives – and to do so it would need to be certain of both the scope of current supply and the nature of likely demand.

Parallel to this, the White Paper also committed the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (no flowers by request) and UKRI to examining “the provision of research activity which delivers against the Industrial Strategy, missions and sovereign capability”, and “assessing changes in capability against our needs.” Given the White Papers interest in using research funding to drive teaching provision, it makes sense to bring these sources of data together.

The dashboard era

I’m hardly one to complain about dashboards as a data analysis and exploration tool – after all, I’ve built one or two in the past. But for me a well-designed dashboard needs to use visualisation and data design to allow the reader to derive an insight that is not available directly from the raw data.

There has been a trend, both in higher education data and in public data more generally, to release data dashboards for public facing information. The canonical examples of excellent practice here are the crime maps that display information to the public about the location, nature, and outcomes of reported crimes.

So when I look at an OfS dashboard, my usual approach is to ask

What insight is this dashboard trying to provide?

What data is it building on?

Does the design use what is in the data to offer the insight that is promised?

Can I use the underlying data to build something that does?

For me, on question 3 the answer is “no, not yet”. That we don’t get the underlying data so we can fix that is annoying, bits that are causing the hold up (the research stuff) is neither interesting nor useful compared to what can be derived from what is already available. I know everyone and their chosen AI life companion is knocking up dashboards and interactives at this point, but the fact that we can chuck all kinds of data up on the same screen doesn’t always mean that we should.

That said, I thought I’d have a go at something providers might find useful. Fire up your big monitor and let me know what you think.

[Full screen]

So this lets you examine a bunch of different datasets by provider and subject. The two yellow filters affect all but one of the visualisations on the dashboard – the exception is the very first one which shows home and current graduate regions using the LEO data set: that’s only available by provider.

The two on the row below are based on UCAS data and work (like the rest of them) by provider and subject. The usual gender, age, and domicile filters are available. On the left we have acceptances, offers and applications as a time series, on the right we have year on year change in that subject area across the sector (there is a flying filter letting you choose your comparator year; this popular chart shows you who is fishing deeply in the pool of available undergraduates, by subject).

Under this is a “cold spot” map by your chosen subject area – you can filter by mode and level and this shows the most recent year of data. There’s a highlighter, or you can mouse over any of the previous charts to highlight the provider you have chosen in the filter.

Right at the bottom we get graduate destinations by provider and subject – there’s filters for the level and mode of the qualification, and the interim study marker.

Data sources

For recruitment we turn, of course, to the UCAS End of Cycle provider data – the most recent release is the 2025 cycle. Though OfS supplements this with student loan take up data from SLC it only seems to do this to provide another perspective on student headcount by subject area, so I’m happy to ignore it at this point.

OfS publishes a size and shape dashboard covering student numbers by provider, and it has some nice features offering a bit more fidelity on entrant status, student domicile and level of study. But HESA DT051 Table 49 offers a UK wide perspective, and I’m not really sure why OfS wants to separate out home funded students given that we as a nation benefit greatly from the skills of international students too.

For student outcomes we could use the B3 release (with the usual caveats about the way indicators are constructed) for completion and continuation – but it is really progression that interests us. For progression there is probably more of interest in graduate outcomes – which allows us to look at what graduates end up doing by provider and subject – and the regional movement stuff available in LEO.

Arguably we should really be looking at course level and at the demand for the skills each course covers. There’s a kind of version of that in this article, but the perils of using the Unistats dataset would make it indicative at best. And arguably we should be able to allocate students, using a course based approach, to individual campuses rather than the main campus in order to build better maps. You can’t get data on student numbers by campus (you can get them by franchise provider which isn’t quite the same thing).

For research I don’t have access to the citation measures from Elsevier, but honestly citation-derived metrics are a hugely limited and deeply problematic proxy for research quality (and I’m still idealistic enough to sign up to the Declaration on Research Assessment) so I don’t mind that much. OfS also uses funding inputs, and staff FTE, but these are only available by cost centre – and given that all the other data I am using defaults to CAH and there are no reliable ways to join the two that also causes a problem.

Fundamentally, while research power is an important thing to think about on a local and regional level (though arguably not in the sense of cold spots as high level research is often commissioned commercially nationally or internationally) I’m not convinced I’m going to easily add much value by adding research data to the student-related stuff at this point. So I’ll deal with it separately.

title: What next for TEF and APP?
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Liz Austen, Associate Dean Learning, Teaching and Student Success and Institutional Lead for the Access and Participation Plan at Sheffield Hallam University. The post What next for TEF and APP? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Liz Austen, Associate Dean Learning, Teaching and Student Success and Institutional Lead for the Access and Participation Plan at Sheffield Hallam University.

The OfS consultation in late 2025 outlined proposals for a future quality system in higher education (England and Wales). These proposals have significant implications for the design and regulation of the Teaching Excellence Framework (TEF), the Access and Participation Plan (APP) and the B Conditions of Registration. The first cohort of new TEF assessments are scheduled for 2027-28 and the sector is still waiting to hear what happens next. Those leading on the strategic delivery of teaching excellence and access and participation, including myself, are particularly interested in how these imminent changes will land.

There are several possible scenarios for how TEF and APP, as existing regulatory submissions, might be integrated. The one that seems most likely is that accountability for the wider range of differential student success outcomes, currently under the APP umbrella of ‘equality of opportunity’, will have a significant place in the TEF. To avoid duplication, the APP will then refocus on access, akin to when OFFA introduced Access Agreements in 2006.

But what does this actually mean? Split metrics by student demographics for most outcomes are already assessed within the TEF, with the TEF narrative playing an important role in explaining any significant contextual factors. However, this is currently a retrospective and defensive narrative to explain current metrics; it does not then formulate a plan to improve them, as the APP currently does.

What if the TEF became a Plan?

Imagine a TEEOP – Teaching Excellence and Equality of Opportunity Plan – has been created, modelled on the existing structure of the APP. In this hypothetical regulatory move, providers are asked to review the OfS Benchmarks for Student Experience, B3 Thresholds Student Outcomes and the Equality of Opportunity Risk Register to consider the various risks that their student population and different groups of students might face. Providers will set timebound and measurable objectives to address these risks. Objectives will be translated into numerical targets, such as

Objective 4c: University x will improve the student responses to NSS questions in the category ‘Teaching on my course’ from 86.1% to 82%.

Intervention strategies will detail how the Provider will meet these student experience, student outcomes and equality of opportunity objectives and an evaluation plan will detail how progress will be monitored and impact reported. A financial report will be submitted to the OfS annually on accountable spend on delivering and evaluating TEEOP interventions. The TEEOP data would be reviewed every 4 years, where new targets would be set and interventions designed. Judgements of excellence would be based on the effectiveness of the Plan and evaluative data reported through the Higher Education Evaluation Library (HEEL).

Considerations

Whilst there are stipulated limitations of not having an APP (e.g. fee caps) and reportable events connected to plan activity and evaluation reporting, no penalties have been applied in the history of the APP. As Jim Dickinson recently noted, APP targets frequently go unmet from one Plan cycle to the next:

Of the 777 assessable targets, 488 – 63 per cent – missed the 2023–24 milestone that the provider had agreed with OfS.

This sits in contrast to the TEF, which is more forthright in the distinction of excellence and has explored the possibilities of sanctions for Bronze or Requires Improvement ratings. If the TEF looked more like the APP, then it would be seriously toning down the regulatory scrutiny and perceived market differentiation of Providers. There are certainly flaws in both these assumptions.

A further challenge is the APP language of ‘intervention’, which is described as a discrete action with a clear beginning and end point, and can be neatly evaluated (Austen in Austen & McCaig, 2025). Actions to improve the student experience are often curriculum based. They might involve course redesign and adaptations in pedagogy and practice. This type of change doesn’t always align to this notion of an ‘intervention’. The NSS is also a flawed measure of impact. This means that the application of APP-style evaluation, and the search for causal evidence historically promoted by TASO, becomes less applicable; a quality process of continuous improvement is more often the means of review, monitoring and evaluation.

A more integrated model would benefit those institutions who are predominantly widening access and securing success for students who are typically underrepresented in higher education. When your APP interventions are more business as usual than targeted, a holistic model of quality regulation is more appealing.

What if the APP became a Framework?

Alternatively, imagine a TEEOF – Teaching Excellence and Equality of Opportunity Framework (for the golf lovers) – is created and modelled on the TEF. In this hypothetical scenario, the OfS sets the number of minimum requirements for Student Experience, Student Outcomes and Equality of Opportunity. The TEF indicators are produced by the OfS and include NSS, continuation, completion, progression, and differential gaps by student group for the most recent 4 years. The TEEOF would include attainment/awarding (good honours) as an additional indicator, previously only included in the APP. OfS set the benchmarks for these indicators. In the TEEOF, this would include sector benchmarks for all differentials, including the ethnicity degree awarding gap, and any other risks to quality of opportunity such as socio-economic disadvantage or care and family responsibilities. Providers obtain a rating of Gold, Silver, Bronze and Requires Improvement based on a panel’s assessment of their indicator data, and a provider narrative submission. A student submission will also be submitted, which specifically includes student voices from students who face risks to equality of opportunity. The TEEOF will assess the quality and equality of undergraduate courses in the first iteration and include postgraduate courses in subsequent years. An indication of the judgements on the feature of excellence would be as follows:

Outstanding quality – signifying features of the student experience, outcomes and equality of opportunity that are among the very highest quality found in the sector for the mix of students and courses taught by a provider

Considerations

The OfS judgements of excellence would explicitly include APP attainment objectives and would include the ethnicity degree awarding gap. As Katharine Hubbard has shown in her HEPI report ‘Making Metrics Matter’,Providers in the current regulatory system are able to obtain TEF Gold while still having substantial Black awarding gaps. Hubbard explicitly concludes that there are ‘multiple TEF Gold and Silver providers with significant racial inequity of outcome’ and of 47 TEF Gold institutions, 7 had Black awarding gaps greater than 25 percentage points. Crucially, this would provide a more authentic appraisal of the quality of provision and would elevate the responsibility to address racial disparities in higher education.

Similarly, but with less enthusiasm than the APP, the TEF does have existing expectations about presenting impact, and references evaluation as a source of this impact evidence. However, this evidence is used as a justification for what has gone before; the TEEOF would not include regulatory expectations for the planned delivery and evaluation of interventions to improve experiences and outcomes. A new set of regulatory guidance, learning from the APP evaluative expectations, could inform Provider narrative submissions.

Conclusions

It is hoped that evaluations of the TEF and the APP, alongside the sector’s consultation responses, have provided a wealth of evidence on a future integrated model. This model should retain those elements that work for both Provider and Regulator, and importantly current and future students. Whether that’s a forward-looking plan or a retrospective account, or a bit of both, remains to be seen.

The post New HEPI Policy Note: ‘Language GCSEs in English schools: a postcode lottery?’ appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Where a pupil goes to school can have a profound impact on whether they get the opportunity to study a language. New HEPI analysis reveals stark geographical and socio-economic inequalities in language learning, with access to German, Latin and other languages particularly limited in many parts of England.

Language GCSEs in English schools: a postcode lottery? (HEPI Policy Note 75) by Megan Bowler, finds that just 4.2% of non-selective state schools average at least one language GCSE entry per pupil. Participation varies dramatically across the country: Hammersmith & Fulham records an average of 0.86 language GCSE entries per pupil, compared with just 0.24 in Blackpool, while seven Local Education Authorities have no GCSE German entries at all. The divide is also strongly associated with disadvantage, with pupils at schools with the highest levels of Free School Meal eligibility considerably less likely to take French, Spanish or German than those at the most advantaged schools.

The Policy Note argues that declining enrolment in university language degrees cannot be understood without considering the limited and unequal opportunities pupils have to study languages at school. It calls for action including making it easier to recruit language teachers from abroad, addressing concerns about exam grading and considering more flexible qualification pathways alongside GCSEs. It also advocates targeted local interventions in areas with particularly low participation and a greater role for universities in supporting language learning through outreach and mentoring.

full_text:
The UK’s biggest education union is claiming a significant victory after the government bowed to pressure and agreed to fully fund a forthcoming pay increase for teachers in England in a sudden U-turn.

Members of the National Education Union (NEU) were due to vote in a ballot for strike action next month over the government’s recent pay offer which provided for a 3.5% increase from this month, with an additional 3% from next September.

While the offer was a significant improvement on initial proposals from the then education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, there was concern among teachers and unions that it was not fully funded and schools would have to find almost a third of the wage increases from existing budgets.

After weeks of negotiation over the summer with the NEU general secretary, Daniel Kebede, Phillipson’s successor, Lucy Powell, confirmed on Wednesday in a letter to the union that the entire pay offer would be fully funded, using funds from recent revaluations of the local government pension scheme.

Kebede said it was a “significant” step and would result in an estimated additional £500m of funding for schools this year, which otherwise would have been spent on the pay rise.

“Finally, we have a government that accepts the reality that any teacher pay award must be fully funded,” he said. “Plugging the £460m black hole in school budgets signals a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community.

“Schools have been running on empty for far too long. Leaders simply could not afford to fund the pay award as set out by the previous education secretary. The new administration has accepted that it is wrong to force schools to make cuts to education just to make ends meet.”

Although the NEU national executive is yet to decide on the fate of the national ballot, the government will be hoping its latest gesture – which it regards not as a change of policy but a change in affordability – will lift the threat of strike action and possible school closures.

In a snap poll before the summer break, 97% of NEU members who participated said it was “unacceptable” that their school would have to find the funds to make up the 1.1% shortfall in government funding of the pay rise, and 89% were prepared to take strike action to ensure the teacher pay award was fully funded.

In her letter to Kebede, Powell said: “I understand you are concerned the funding available in 26-27 is insufficient to cover the costs of the recent pay award.

“I am therefore pleased to be able to update you that recent revaluations to the local government pension scheme will see a 4.9ppt reduction in employer contribution rates and deliver significant savings on schools’ pay bill for support staff.

“We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.”

She added: “Given the material change to the affordability position, I would ask that the NEU revisits its proposed ballot of members planned for October and moves away from strike action.”

Luke Sibieta, a research fellow at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the government’s announcement amounted to a £500m boost to school funding in England, which equated to a permanent increase of just under 1%. “Coming on top of other funding increases, this means that from next year schools will be £1.6bn better off than they had expected to be this summer.”

A spokesperson for Powell said later that the education secretary “has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities.

“High-quality teaching is the single most important in-school factor in improving outcomes for children, which is why this government has backed the profession with a pay award that recognises teachers’ vital role.”

Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the NASUWT teachers’ union, said: “Finally the government has seen sense and started to address the issue we have been raising for months around the funding of the teachers’ pay award.”

title: Beyond Financial Aid for First-Gen Students
summary:
Beyond Financial Aid for First-Gen Students Joshua.Bay Wed, 09/16/2026 - 03:00 AM The Kessler Scholars Collaborative pairs financial aid with mentoring, as well as community and individualized support. An Ithaka S+R evaluation shows promising outcomes. Byline(s) Joshua Bay Beyond Financial Aid for First-Gen Students
Joshua.Bay Wed, 09/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

The Kessler Scholars Collaborative pairs financial aid with mentoring, as well as community and individualized support. An Ithaka S+R evaluation shows promising outcomes.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
First-generation students make up 54 percent of all undergraduates in the U.S., but only 24 percent attain a bachelor’s degree within six years, compared with 59 percent of their continuing-generation peers, according to FirstGen Forward. The Kessler Scholars Collaborative has sought to close the degree-attainment gap through a comprehensive support model for first-gen students.

The collaborative was formed in 2020 to back programs at six inaugural institutions, including the University of Michigan, where the first Kessler Scholars Program was established in 2008. In 2022, 10 additional institutions were selected to join the collaborative as part of a partnership with the American Talent Initiative.

Supported by Bloomberg Philanthropies and the Wilpon Family Foundation, the program offers first-generation, limited-income students financial aid plus community, mentoring and individualized guidance. Nearly 1,200 students participated during the 2025–26 academic year, and the program expects to serve nearly 1,500 this fall, including 392 new scholars.

An external evaluation from Ithaka S+R looked at how Kessler Scholars are faring compared with other first-generation students at the same institutions. Among Kessler Scholars who entered the six inaugural institutions in fall 2020, 74 percent earned bachelor’s degrees within four years, compared with an average of 59 percent of all first-generation students at the same institutions. By the end of summer 2025, 84 percent of the Kessler cohort had earned a degree.

“One of the metrics that we’re looking closely at is not just do students on these campuses outperform the national first-gen metrics on persistence and completion—which are troublingly low—but because we’re working with campuses that are so diverse, are they also outperforming first-gen students on their campuses?” said Gail Gibson, executive director of the Kessler Scholars Program.

She added that the program also focuses on helping students access academic and professional opportunities that can prepare them for success after graduation.

“Kessler helps unveil the ‘hidden curriculum’ of higher ed,” Gibson said. “The program thinks about the hidden curriculum of the workplace and how we prepare students for internships, research experiences and other opportunities that mean the success they found on campus can repeat after graduation.”

How Kessler works: Among graduating seniors surveyed at the six inaugural institutions, 81 percent participated in at least one of three high-impact experiences: an internship, undergraduate research or study abroad. Specifically, 59 percent had completed an internship, 49 percent had participated in faculty-mentored research and 40 percent had studied abroad.

“We’re trying to make the case that ‘Yes, you are talented and smart, and we want you in these institutions, but we don’t want you to crawl through and finish without the same sort of rich experiences that your peers have,’” Gibson said. “High-impact practices are a really strong example of that.”

The evaluation also found that 85 percent of survey respondents in 2024–25 said they felt they belonged within their Kessler community and 88 percent felt that they mattered to the program.

Nick Watson, program lead for college access and success at Bloomberg Philanthropies, said the community-building component is one of the most important elements of the collaborative.

“Being a first-gen and limited-income student and having someone who’s gone through the experience to then tell you ‘Actually you do belong’ and build connection—it’s part of the secret sauce here,” Watson said. “That seems like a no-brainer, but so many times institutions take it for granted that it’s happening organically or naturally.”

Kessler Scholars at the inaugural institutions had an average cumulative GPA of 3.40, compared with 3.12 among other first-generation students at the same institutions. Ithaka cautioned that its comparisons between Kessler Scholars and other first-generation students are descriptive and do not account for differences in students’ precollege characteristics or other factors that could influence selection into the program.

For Watson, one benefit of expanding the collaborative is the opportunity to examine how the model works across a range of institutions from an Ivy League university like Brown University to a smaller institution like Centre College.

“What can we learn when we pair varied institutions together about what makes this work?” Watson said. “What we’ve seen is you have to have institutions that are coming in from the same student-centered space.”

Gibson said participating institutions are expected to provide a consistent set of core supports but have the flexibility to adapt the program to their own students and campus context. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, for example, has used Kessler to focus on recruiting rural students from across the state, while Washington University in St. Louis has prioritized persistence among first-generation students majoring in STEM fields.

“There are core elements of the program model that we ask each institution to implement,” Gibson said. “Students should have a peer mentor, there should be a dedicated staff person, students should come together for rich and unique cohort-based activities. This is, after all, a community-driven intervention.”

“But local context should control, and without it, you’re not going to have the kind of learning, institutional buy-in and meaning if that weren’t true,” she added.

Lessons for other institutions: The evaluation also identified areas for improvement. Some 55 percent of scholars met with program staff at least twice per semester, while 57 percent attended at least three Kessler events per semester. Sustaining engagement as students progress through college remains an ongoing challenge for the program, Ithaka noted.

Gibson said additional data expected in spring 2027 will offer a first look at outcomes across all 16 participating institutions.

For institutions outside the collaborative looking to strengthen support for first-generation students, Watson said the lesson isn’t necessarily to replicate Kessler in its entirety, but to start small and build from there.

“It doesn’t have to look the same at every place. But there are learnings for all types of institutions, depending on where you’re at, both from a bandwidth perspective and also a resource perspective,” Watson said.

Gibson said institutions can look to models like Kessler for strategies they can adapt to address the particular challenges facing first-generation students on their campuses.

“This question about ‘How do we get smarter and better at student success?’ is one that schools are wrestling with across higher ed right now,” Gibson said. “One reason we’ve emphasized evaluation—especially external evaluation—throughout is because we want this project to be able to offer guidance and learning across the sector.”

title: The 'burnerverse' exploiting young women in college
summary: Wired reporter EJ Dickson speaks with NPR's Juana Summers about an online community that targets and harasses young women with their own nonconsensual, sexually explicit images.
full_text:
Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

People call it the burnerverse. It's a loosely connected online community of sports fans. But this anonymous corner of the internet doesn't just talk smack about the athletes they don't like or complain about their team's most recent losses. They have also doxed young women, making their names and nonconsensual explicit videos or images viral on platforms like X and subjecting them to online harassment. Ej Dickson is a senior cultural reporter for Wired magazine, and she recently wrote about this corner of the internet and joins me now to talk about it. Hi there.

EJ DICKSON: Hi. Thank you for having me.

SUMMERS: Thanks for being here. Ej, for people who have never heard of the burnerverse before, what is it, and where did it come from?

DICKSON: Well, it's ostensibly a community of college sports fan accounts that are anonymous. And I want to be clear, it's not representative of the whole community. There are a lot of burner accounts that are pretty innocuous, but there is a segment of the community that is pretty violently racist, misogynistic and antisemitic and that has made something of a sport out of doxing young women.

SUMMERS: You mentioned that this is a community of college sports fans. Do we have a sense of how big these burner communities are and who's actually participating in them?

DICKSON: It's hard to gauge how big it is because it's so sprawling and it's loosely connected. And every college or university that has a big sports team will have, like, its own little burner galaxy, as it were. The second part of your question - who belongs to the burnerverse? - it's pretty wide-ranging. I was shocked when I started digging into who is behind these accounts. It's men in their 20s, 30s, 40s, men who are long out of college. It really could be anybody.

SUMMERS: Your article focuses on the story of a young woman named Maddie Kowalski who found herself at the center of a burnerverse campaign. Tell us what happened to her.

DICKSON: Maddie Kowalski was a University of Florida sophomore last November when she discovered that a bunch of intimate images had been leaked nonconsensually of her. And at first, it was just within her college campus and then within the Florida college community. But then it got posted by these burner accounts and it went viral nationally.

SUMMERS: In recent years, victims of revenge porn now have more legal recourse. All 50 states now have laws that criminalize the nonconsensual distribution of intimate images. And last year, President Trump signed the TAKE IT DOWN Act into law, which made it a federal crime to knowingly share or even threaten to share intimate images, including deepfakes. But as we've been talking about, the burnerverse is mostly anonymous, so for women like Maddie Kowalski, is there actually any legal recourse in this situation because we don't know who these people are?

DICKSON: There is. Thanks to the Florida sexual cyberharassment statute, there was legal recourse for Maddie specifically. And thanks to the TAKE IT DOWN Act, there is legal recourse for a lot of these victims. But it takes time.

SUMMERS: Lots of women have been doxed online over the years for various reasons. As someone who covers the culture, what does this tell you about the ways the internet and its culture are changing?

DICKSON: I think the cultural and political climate is definitely playing a role, but there are also so many other little things contributing to this. It's the lack of regulation on platforms like X. It's the incredibly slow pace of our legal institutions, of these universities that see this happening. Like, these institutions are really not keeping pace with how fast the internet is changing, and I think this piece is a pretty harrowing demonstration of that.

SUMMERS: We've been speaking with Ej Dickson. Her investigation, titled "A College Girl Was Exploited On Camera. A Network Of Anonymous Men Got To Work," is available to read from Wired magazine. Ej, thanks for your reporting.

DICKSON: Thank you so much.

title: School absence up among disadvantaged students - study
summary: School absence has increased among young people with socio-emotional difficulties and those who do not like school in the last 10 years, research has shown.
full_text:
School absence has increased among young people with socio-emotional difficulties and those who do not like school in the last 10 years, research has shown.

New research, published by the ESRI and produced in partnership with Tusla, uses Growing Up in Ireland (GUI) data to trace patterns of absence from nine to 13 years of age, identifying the individual, family and school factors that contribute to school absence.

Among the key findings were that absence rates vary significantly by social background, with higher rates among unskilled manual and non-employed families, those whose mothers have lower levels of education, families experiencing financial strain and lone-parent households.

It also stated that national data revealed higher rates of school absence in Ireland since the pandemic, as has been found in many other countries.

It further found that young people with a disability are much more likely to miss school than their peers.

Young people for whom a disability emerged or was identified between nine and 13 years tend to have increasing absence rates.

The research found that young people are more likely to miss school if their parents have a harsher parenting style, for example, shouting at their child rather than explaining things, and there is a lack of routine around bedtimes and breakfast.

Experiencing adverse life events like bereavement or addiction is a significant predictor of school absence.

There are higher absence rates in DEIS schools, because of the concentration of socio-economic disadvantage in these schools, while schools that involve students to a greater extent in decision-making tend to have lower absence rates.

Absence rates are higher among young people with negative attitudes to school at nine and/or 13 years, those who have poorer quality relationships with their teachers and those who experienced bullying at age nine.

The findings stated that absence rates vary across areas, and are higher among young people living in rented accommodation and those living in areas with low social capital, including poorer facilities for teens.

National data show higher rates of school absence in Ireland since the pandemic, as has been found in many other countries.

GUI data allowed researchers to compare two cohorts of 13-year-olds a decade apart, with the cohort in 2008 making the transition to post-primary education over the pandemic.

Absence rates are stable at age nine but increase significantly among 13-year-olds post-pandemic.

Greater socio-emotional difficulties are found among young people now than a decade earlier. This increase has played an important role in driving a growth in absence levels.

Not liking school is also a more strongly predictive of absence than previously.

'Range of factors' influencing school absence - report author

Emer Smyth, co-author of the report, said: "The findings point to the range of factors that influence school absence, so policy responses need to be multi-dimensional and integrated.

"Schools can make a difference by fostering positive attitudes to school, greater student involvement and reducing negative teacher-student and peer interaction to enhance attendance."

Anna Moya, co-author of the report, said: "The strong association found between socio-economic disadvantage at family and area level and school absence highlights the need for broader anti-child poverty policy to bolster educational interventions.

"Mental health and parenting support services are also needed to assist families through challenging life events."

Áine O'Keeffe, national service director of Tusla Education Support Service, said: "In commissioning this report TESS set out to contribute to our understanding of the interplay of individual, family, school and community factors that impact on regular school attendance in Ireland.

"Through our front line teams, TESS continues to work directly with children, young people, families and schools to support improved school attendance."

title: Why a softer student market demands a connected education journey
summary:
As international student demand softens, a more connected approach to preparation, language, pathways and university guidance could help students navigate an increasingly complex journey.

The post Why a softer student market demands a connected education journey appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
International education is commonly organised around separate products: test preparation, English tuition, academic pathways and university applications. Students, however, experience one journey, often beginning years before an overseas application.

Families are deciding earlier and asking harder questions about readiness, progression and value. Universities need applicants prepared for international study. Yet the handover between specialist providers is often weak.

Why a softer market changes the opportunity

International student demand is becoming softer and more uneven. UK sponsored study visa grants in the year ending March 2026 were lower than the previous year and remained below their 2023 peak. Canada reported substantially lower demand for new study permits during 2025, while Australia recorded lower overall enrolments and commencements in early 2026, despite higher education growth.

Demand has not disappeared; it has become more selective and sensitive to policy, affordability and confidence

Demand has not disappeared; it has become more selective and sensitive to policy, affordability and confidence. When applications are under pressure, organisations cannot rely only on reaching students at the point of recruitment. They must engage earlier, build readiness and provide clearer progression routes. This creates an opportunity to connect preparation, language development, pathways and university guidance within one coordinated model.

Connecting preparation with progression

A student considering the United States may begin with SAT preparation. Another may need academic English or IELTS support. Some require an A-Level or foundation pathway before university selection and applications. When each stage is handled separately, advice can become inconsistent and preparation gaps may be identified too late.

Westminster International Group is developing an education ecosystem around this journey. The SAT School supports SAT and international qualification preparation. Westminster School of English provides language programmes and IELTS preparation, while AiELTS adds digital practice, mock examinations and AI-supported feedback. Westminster College Bangkok provides secondary, pre-university and higher education pathways, and WIN Education supports university selection, applications and admissions guidance.

Bringing these capabilities under one roof allows engagement to begin earlier and continue more coherently. The value is not simply more products, but the right support at the right time. Families gain clearer decisions, schools can complement existing support, and universities can receive better-informed applicants with more realistic expectations.

For the model to work, however, technology must support rather than replace experienced teachers and advisers. Trust also depends on recommending only the services each learner genuinely needs, rather than moving students automatically between internal programmes.

Taking the model into new markets

As Westminster International Group develops this model, I am pleased to announce Pradeep Singh Adhikari as global sales director. With more than 16 years’ experience in international education and partnerships, he will grow WIN Education’s presence in India and South Asia and adapt the model to different student and institutional needs.

Commenting on his appointment, Pradeep said: “I am pleased to join WIN Education at a stage when students and families need clearer, connected support. My immediate priority is to grow our presence in India and South Asia and work with universities, education partners and franchise operators that share our commitment to responsible recruitment and positive student outcomes.”

Saf Jeevanjee, global business development director, added: “Having worked with Pradeep before, I am completely confident in his capability to interweave practical experience, market insights and performance excellence into the execution of a formidable global sales and recruitment strategy. It is great to be working with him again, as we chart the growth of Westminster International Group to new heights, supporting our regional teams to build sustainable international partnerships.”

International education’s future will depend on connecting early preparation, language development, pathways and university guidance while keeping advice personal, transparent and focused on student outcomes.

title: Universities are talking to students. Students are talking to AI
summary:
AI is completely changing the way students research universities. So how can institutions get ahead of those changes and avoid being left behind, asks Georgia Spanou.

The post Universities are talking to students. Students are talking to AI appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
A 17-year-old in Berlin or Seoul deciding where to study abroad no longer starts with a brochure. She opens ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, types “best universities in Europe for business psychology with good job outcomes and a stable visa route”, and gets a shortlist in eight seconds, with no admissions office built and no marketing budget touched.

That shortlist is the real front door of international education now, and most institutions haven’t noticed.

The funnel has a new gatekeeper

For 20 years, international recruitment has been a game of visibility: rank well, show up on page one, get the click. That game assumed a human was clicking. Increasingly, they’re not.

An EAB survey of over 5,000 US high schoolers found 46% now use tools like ChatGPT during their college search, nearly double the 26% recorded in spring 2025, and one in five had already dropped an institution based on what AI told them. INTO University Partnerships’ own survey of 1,600 newly enrolled international students found something more uncomfortable: 96% of enrolled students who used AI said it matched or exceeded official sources.

For 20 years, international recruitment has been a game of visibility: rank well, show up on page one, get the click. That game assumed a human was clicking. Increasingly, they’re not

Marketing teams have spent a decade optimising for Google’s algorithm. Now they need to be legible to a reader that doesn’t click through and forms its answer by synthesising whatever it finds, accurately represented or not. Higher ed marketers are already scrambling to adapt, chasing what’s now called generative or answer engine optimisation. But GEO isn’t a new marketing channel. It’s a new buyer sitting between the institution and the student, and most universities have no idea what it’s been told to say about them.

This isn’t abstract to me. Our own enrollment data this year showed 80% of the EU and US students who enrolled with us first found out we existed through Claude or ChatGPT, not our website or paid campaigns. Credibility has relocated into the AI-mediated layer now sitting between us and the student.

The questions we can’t yet answer

Here’s what unsettles me most: we don’t know why the algorithm is choosing us, and we’re building strategy around it anyway. Is what makes a model treat information as credible thesame discipline SEO demanded, or has the ground moved toward the forums these models lean on, Reddit included?

A second question troubles me too: our AI-driven enquiries skew heavily toward wealthier, English-speaking markets. Are the models steering higher-income users toward private institutions like ours, by design or their training data, or is this an adoption gap that will close over time?

I don’t have a clean answer to either question, and I’d be suspicious of anyone who claims they do. What we do have is a growing pile of decisions, where we invest, which markets we chase, shaped by systems whose logic none of us can fully see. That should trouble this sector more than it does.

The weight of choosing

The same students turning to AI are actively hostile to institutional marketing. EAB found more than half reacted negatively the moment they suspected a college’s message had been written, or polished, by AI. They want machine-verified facts and human-sounding trust, and are getting good at telling the two apart.

That distrust makes sense given what this generation carries: told that platforms and data would make the right choice obvious, and finding neither delivers. Faced with too many options and too little certainty, students either get overwhelmed or hand their judgement to the algorithm, not for convenience but to avoid the blame alone.

But that isn’t the whole story. What’s driving students toward AI isn’t only fear of a bad decision, it’s a need for personal attention. As AI usage among our prospective students has climbed this year, our WhatsApp channel has filled up alongside it, not emptied out. Students want guidance tailored to them, and they’ll take it from whoever answers first and means it.

This is the psychology of the student as a buyer, shifting faster than most recruitment strategies can track. A generation raised on synthetic content doesn’t reward polish; it rewards proof and being heard. Peer testimony and a real person on the other end of a message now outperform a polished campus video. The brand isn’t the message. The evidence is.

The algorithm is watching geopolitics too

The third force is one the sector can’t optimise its way around: the shortlist a chatbot produces is shaped in real time by policy volatility. In the US, visa issuance to Indian and Chinese students fell roughly 60% and 46% this summer versus the 2017-2025 average, and NAFSA data shows new international enrolments falling 20% year-on-year this spring.

New September rules add a four-year completion cap and halve the post-study grace period. None of that is abstractpolicy to a model trained on current news, it’s a live input reshaping what “safe” and “worth it” mean.

Consultant Vincenzo Raimo calls it a “realignment” toward Europe, toward transnational education, toward markets that look stable rather than prestigious. An algorithm has no institutional loyalty; it reads volatility and adjusts the answer.

Multiple forces, one shift

Put together, this isn’t separate trends, it’s one. The student-as-buyer no longer trusts the seller’s own voice, so they’ve handed decision-making weight to a machine intermediary that at least sounds attentive. That machine, in turn, is reading a world of visa reversals and shifting alliances, updating its advice before a communications team drafts a statement.

The question this raises isn’t tactical. It’s existential. Institutions have spent years asking how to market more effectively to seventeen-year-olds. The sharper question is who, or what, is making the decision on their behalf, and whether anyone here has had a say in what it’s been told.

title: US institutions dominate global MBA rankings
summary:
US universities continue to dominate the global MBA landscape, taking the top four spots in the newly released QS Global MBA and Business Master’s 2027 Rankings.

The post US institutions dominate global MBA rankings appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
For the first time, MIT Sloan has been crowned the world’s best MBA, followed by Harvard Business School, Stanford Graduate School of Business, Penn (Wharton) and Cambridge (Judge), rounding out the top five in the latest rankings from QS Quacquarelli Symonds.

QS president Nunzio Quacquarelli said the rankings showed that the US remained the “powerhouse” of graduate management education, home to 11 of the top 20 MBA programs.

“This year has shown that specialised Business Master’s programs are becoming more competitive, with US institutions maintaining a lead, particularly in Business Analytics and Supply Chain Management,” said Quacquarelli.

The data, which analyses the world’s 420+ best global MBAs and a series of specialised business master’s across 65 countries, featured a total of 150 American institutions, with entries for both categories growing compared to last year.

Meanwhile, the average salary in the US after graduating with an MBA is also on the rise, increasing from $110,286 in 2026 to $115,492 in 2027.

But Quacquarelli said: “Where US institutions are losing out to global peers is in return on the investment, with European institutions continuing to excel in the area.”

Where US institutions are losing out to global peers is in return on the investment

Nunzio Quacquarelli, QS

The UK was the second most represented country, with 42 institutions appearing in the rankings, followed by France with 35, India with 28 and Canada and Spain each with 24.

The world’s premier MBA program at MIT (Sloan) climbed from third place last year, leading on Employability and Thought Leadership, and coming third in Entrepreneurship and Alumni Outcomes – measuring which schools are associated with the world’s largest countries and students starting their own companies.

Elsewhere, Chicago (Booth) made it back into the top 10, recognised for Employability, Entrepreneurship and Return on Investment (ROI), though no US entry ranks in the top 10 globally for ROI or Diversity.

title: Number of new international grad students soars in Canada
summary:
A new Canadian government initiative to attract more graduate students is paying off, with the number of study permits issued to them doubling this spring compared to 2025.

The post Number of new international grad students soars in Canada appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says it issued 6,455 new grad students permits in the second quarter of 2026, the latest period for which data is available. That compares to 3,085 in 2025.

The jump came even as the overall number of applications fell slightly. In the second quarter of this year, 23,480 international grad students sought a new or extended study permit, down about 12% from the same period last year.

Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the government has changed its international student focus to attract master’s and PhD students to Canada. “We recognise that we need them here to grow our economy,” IRCC minister Lena Metlege Diab told a meeting in Halifax in January.

Canada implemented a cap on the number of international study permits in 2024, with then-minister Marc Miller arguing that some programs were the educational equivalent of “puppy mills”. Many international students weren’t even attending classes, he claimed.

Prior to the cap, some college and university undergrad programs were recruiting international students to help meet their budget challenges. Overseas students pay much higher tuition fees than Canadians; therefore, each international student generates more revenue.

IRCC spokesperson Melissa Zeroual says the new policy is reflected in study permit approvals this year. “The number of study permits issued to master’s and doctoral students represented 12% of the total in 2025 – and 21% so far this year.”

While many universities won’t report their grad student enrolment figures until the end of the year, the University of British Columbia (UBC) is one school that said the number of applications is up.

The number of study permits issued to master’s and doctoral students represented 12% of the total in 2025 – and 21% so far this year

Melissa Zeroual, IRCC

“International graduate student applications have increased 15% in 2026, with a 30% increase for doctoral programs,” said Shane Moore, marketing and recruitment manager in the faculty of graduate and postdoctoral studies. UBC cites strong interest among students from the United States, India, Nigeria and Iran.

Earlier this year, the Liberal government exempted grad students from the requirement to have a Provincial or Territorial Attestation Letter (PAL or TAL). These letters show that a province or territory has accounted for the student under its allocation of study permits for the year.

“This exemption removes an administrative barrier for graduate students in recognition of their unique contribution to Canada’s economic growth and innovation,” said Zeroual.

The government has also promised PhD applicants that their paperwork will be processed within 14 days.

The increase in foreign grad students is not a temporary phenomenon, Zeroual said. “IRCC is expecting this trend to continue with new measures directed at graduate students in 2026 and a continued focus on attracting talent at the master’s and PhD level.”

Robert Asselin, head of the U15 organisation of Canada’s top research universities, says the growth is “great news because we need more grad students, especially at the doctoral level.”

He credits Prime Minister Carney’s efforts to build international partnerships in the wake of US President Donald Trump’s threats to Canadian sovereignty. “This has had a tremendous impact on our brand and our attractiveness to international students,” Asselin said.

title: 2026 Global Impact Grants spotlight AI innovation and inclusion across higher education

13 universities across four continents have been recognised in this year’s Global Impact Grants, Advance HE’s annual funding opportunity to share good practice in higher education, with case studies ranging from AI-assisted teaching to targeted support for care-experienced students.

We’re delighted to share the case studies from the 2025/26 round of Global Impact Grants. The collection spans institutions in Australia, Vietnam, Ireland, the Netherlands, Malaysia, China and Mauritius, reflecting the international breadth of innovation taking place across the sector.

AI generates innovation

Artificial intelligence features heavily among this year’s winners. At Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in China, researchers built an ‘agentic AI’ tool, InQ2Plan, to help academics design action research projects, moving beyond an earlier chatbot that staff found too rigid for specific queries.

A collaboration between the University of Nottingham Malaysia, Sunway University and the University of Nottingham UK examined how institutions can move past outright bans on generative AI towards more coherent policy. Drawing on surveys and interviews with staff and students, the project built a framework intended to embed AI use in assessment in ways that are authentic, inclusive and sustainable.

Focus on inclusivity

Across other themes, at the University of Galway in Ireland a dedicated support role for care-experienced students has helped lift progression rates and cut withdrawals, from 12% in 2023-24 to 8% in 2025-26. The initiative, built on partnerships with organisations including Tusla and the Irish Foster Care Association, has since fed into a new national network, the Care Experienced Educational Network of Ireland.

Elsewhere, a joint project between Srinakharinwirot University in Thailand and Breda University of Applied Sciences in the Netherlands used a ‘living lab’ model to address long-running conflict between local communities and elephants around Kuiburi National Park.

Other case studies in the collection cover doctoral wellbeing, gamified learning, academic onboarding and intercultural collaboration, at institutions including Queensland University of Technology, RMIT University, Adelaide University, Monash University and the Open University of Mauritius.

title: Democratising employability: the live brief revolution
summary: The post Democratising employability: the live brief revolution appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Falmouth University Senior Lecturer, Lucy Cokes, shares an updated practical seven-tier model to make student industry experience equitable, manageable and scalable.

We are facing an equity crisis in higher education employability. In today’s challenging economic climate, plagued by a persistent cost-of-living crisis, students simply do not have the luxury of undertaking unpaid, extracurricular internships or portfolios, building placements in their spare time.

If professional experience is kept outside the classroom, we inadvertently lock out a massive portion of our student body – particularly those working part-time to survive, or those managing commuting and caring responsibilities.

To make social mobility a reality, we must change our practice. We must design our curricula to bring the real world directly into their timetabled, assessed hours.

The “missing tier” of live briefs

When I first proposed the Hierarchy of Live Briefs in late 2024, my goal was to spark a dialogue about structural equity in curriculum design. I wanted to move the sector away from ad-hoc, selective industry projects.

Two years on, that dialogue has turned into a quiet revolution. At Falmouth University, the hierarchy is printed in A3 and stuck on our staff room wall – a daily visual anchor during our day-to-day work.

However, scholarship is iterative. It was during a collaborative meeting with a fellow academic that a glaring omission in my original framework was pointed out. I had focused heavily on the “gold standard” of paid, produced client work, completely bypassing the very level that busy academics use most regularly: briefs that are unpaid, embedded in assessment, with the ideas pitched to the client. So a new tier has been added to the hierarchy.

In this scenario, a real client provides a brief, and students gain the vital experience of pitching and receiving industry feedback. Because there is no client budget, the work does not go into commercial production.

Omitting this was a mistake as this tier is the absolute mainstay of equitable industry engagement. It preserves fairness, ensuring every single student participates within scheduled hours, while remaining highly achievable for course teams regardless of their discipline’s funding landscape.

Simplifying the choice: a three-question diagnostic

Ultimately, the hierarchy is about giving course leaders simple, manageable options. To strip away the academic jargon, we can map any live brief by answering three binary questions shown in the decision matrix below:

This validates Tier C as an incredibly valuable, highly equitable teaching tool, while giving course teams a realistic roadmap to try and push projects up to a Tier B or A in the future.

Dismantling the operational bottleneck

The biggest barrier to embedding live briefs in higher education is rarely pedagogical, however, it is operational. Creative academics are brilliant educators, but they often freeze when confronted with the legal and administrative hurdles of live projects. How do we handle intellectual property (IP)? How do we write client agreements? How do we map chaotic real-world timelines to rigid 12-week academic blocks? Many staff stop at the first or second hurdle.

Before transitioning to academia, I spent years as a digital agency founder and corporate Chief Operations Officer (COO) managing 80 staff. Systems, contracts and budgets are second nature to me. Having spent years navigating our university’s complex internal bureaucracy to build a repeatable, safe path, I felt a responsibility to share the blueprint I had created.

At our annual staff training event this June, we launched a dedicated Live Brief resource page on our Staff Intranet. It features ready to use templates, including pre-approved client and IP handover agreements and costing estimators. By lowering the administrative barrier to entry, we have seen a dramatic increase in staff confidence. It has turned our staff room poster from an aspirational target into an actionable checklist.

What the data tells us

We must practice what we teach. Over the past academic year, I have gathered quantitative and qualitative data from six different modules at Falmouth University that have actively embedded live briefs.

The early indicators from our employability research are incredibly clear: students working on embedded live briefs report a significantly higher sense of professional agency, improved portfolio confidence and a clearer understanding of how their skills translate to the workplace. Crucially, this boost is felt equally across all demographics, proving that embedding these opportunities directly in modules is a vital tool for social mobility.

Our next step is to take this data-driven blueprint on the road to deliver training workshops at universities across the country. If we want to prepare our young people for the future of work, we have to make our curriculum look more like the world they are entering.

Are you currently using live briefs in your teaching? Where do your modules sit in the seven-tier hierarchy?

Lucy Cokes is a Senior Lecturer in Advertising at Falmouth University, a Senior Fellow of Advance HE and founder of ‘Be Good’, an in-house behaviour change agency. Previously a digital agency founder and corporate COO, she researches the impact of professional agency on student social mobility.

title: Il coaching scopre l’AI: cresce l’uso, mancano regole condivise

full_text:
L’Intelligenza Artificiale è ormai entrata a far parte della cassetta degli attrezzi delle professioni più eterogenee ed è destinata a rimanerci, compresi quei settori in cui la componente umana è alla base della professione stessa.
